#ArchCanvas #FloorPlans #SelfBuild #HomeDesign #CAD

A curved wall is where drawing-by-code usually gives up. You get a many-sided polygon that looks smooth until you zoom in.

So I drew the West Wing's first floor in ArchLang, mostly to see what the Oval Office would do.

The bow is one clause inside the wall statement: two endpoints, a radius of 7300 mm, and the word cw — which decides whether the facade bulges out into the Rose Garden or caves inward.

What comes out is a real arc: two arc commands in the sheet, the wall's inner and outer faces at that radius plus and minus half its 300 mm thickness, nothing faceted at any zoom. The three south windows are written at 25%, 50% and 75%, and a percentage on a curve walks by arc length rather than the chord, so they land on even quarters of the bow. No trigonometry in the source.

The floor is 24 rooms and 1,568.98 m², an A1 sheet at 1:100, and the linter comes back clean.

An original illustration based on publicly available floor plans, not an official record — the room names and relationships are the documented ones, the dimensions plausible rather than surveyed.

Plan, source and notes: https://lnkd.in/ewrEPU-j — repo at https://lnkd.in/ejMuh5Hv

#ArchLang #FloorPlans #OpenSource #Architecture #DeveloperTools

The West Wing first-floor plan with three callouts: the Oval Office bow drawn as one arc clause, the Cabinet Room's table and fourteen chairs from a single loop, and the windowless Roosevelt Room at the centre of the plan.
The clean compiled floor plan: 24 named and dimensioned rooms in three bands, a numbered grid, a north arrow and a title block, with the Oval Office bowing out at the lower right.

posts.text:
Most AI floor plans look right at a glance.

Then a wall stops a few centimetres short. A door's drawn too narrow. The room sizes don't quite add up. The picture looked fine — the plan underneath didn't hold.

ArchCanvas designs one strong, dimensioned floor plan from a plain-English brief: walls that actually close, dimensions that hold. Then it refines that plan with you until it's right.

The bet is deliberate — one consistent plan you shape for free beats several rough options you choose between blind. If it's the wrong bet for you, the free tier costs nothing to find out.

Two honest things, because this page won't do hype:
• A plan takes about 100–160 seconds. We compile and check the geometry before you see it.
• You get a concept plan to act on and hand to a professional — not a stamped permit set. It shrinks the architect's bill; it doesn't dodge it.

No subscription. You pay per result you keep, with credits that never expire.
